5--- # Hoare2: Hoare Logic, Part II
6-
7-open scoped Com MyGetElem Assertion HasTriple
8-
9--- Note to developers (before next release):
10---     BCP 23,25: There are a lot of questions about the flow of this
11---     material. Needs a deep look. In particular:
12---
13---     - One feels that it takes a rather circuitous route to get to formal
14---       decorated programs -- there might be a way to just go straight there.
15---       More importantly, it isn't very clear to me that the version of
16---       decorated programs that we wound up with is really the right one -- why
17---       spend all this time writing annotations that we then say are
18---       unnecessary? Seems like we could define decorated programs with a
19---       lighter annotation burden (as in the exercise at the end) and just add
20---       optional annotations when we want to, to make particular examples
21---       clearer.
22---
23---     - The rigidity of the Hoare rules as stated in the last chapter is also
24---       annoying here at many points. Building the rules of consequence into
25---       all the other rules might make a lot of things smoother. Would be a big
26---       change (also to Hoare.v), but definitely worth a try.
27---
28---     And related...
29-
30--- Note to developers (Michael Clarkson @clarksmr, before next release, 2020):
31---     Here are a bunch of improvements I wanted to make but didn't have time
32---     to get to. Maybe next time if no one else gets to them first.
33---
34---     - 1. This chapter feels largely disconnected from the style of the rest of
35---          the series, which is "100% Rocq script". There's a significant amount
36---          of "just comments" here instead. I think we could make this much better
37---          by introducing formal decorated programs right after we informally
38---          define them. Then in the examples that follow do each informal
39---          decorated program (to get students to find the right assertions, more
40---          or less) followed immediately by a formal version, instead of delaying
41---          formal so far to the end. The `parity` exercise is a good example of
42---          one that already almost does this already. (BCP 21: Done!)
43---
44---     - 2. There are several places where we are verifying Imp program schemas,
45---          not actual programs. We're mixing Rocq variables with Imp variables.
46---          That's confusing. One example is `two_loops`; I've tried to mark others
47---          as I come across them. (BCP: I've added some quizzes and such to try to
48---          clarify the relation between programs / triples and program/triple
49---          schemas. BCP 25: I think this is a non-issue now.)
50---
51---     - 3. Weakest preconditions show up in this chapter as completely optional,
52---          then are revisited (and required) in HoareAsLogic. Consider moving the
53---          entire treatment to that chapter. (BCP 23: Yes, we should do that!)
54---
55---     - 4. It seems a shame that the SparseAnnotations section is not visible in
56---          the full version, but only in a solution. It's fantastic! It would be
57---          great to show it off. (BCP 25: Yes! Indeed, perhaps it should even
58---          replace the current treatment!)
59-

109--- ## Decorated Programs
110-
111--- The beauty of Hoare Logic is that it is *syntax directed*: the structure of
112--- proofs exactly follows the structure of programs.
113-
114--- We can record the essential ideas of a Hoare-logic proof — omitting
115--- low-level calculational details — by "decorating" a program with
116--- appropriate assertions on each of its commands.
117-
118--- Such a *decorated program* carries within itself an argument for its own
119--- correctness.
120-
121--- For example, consider the program:
122-
123---   X := m;
124---   Z := p;
125---   while X <> 0 do
126---     Z := Z - 1;
127---     X := X - 1
128---   end
129-
130--- Here is one possible specification for this program, in the form of a Hoare
131--- triple:
132-
133---   {{ True }}
134---   X := m;
135---   Z := p;
136---   while X <> 0 do
137---     Z := Z - 1;
138---     X := X - 1
139---   end
140---   {{ Z = p - m }}
141-
142--- (Note the *parameters* `m` and `p`, which stand for fixed-but-arbitrary
143--- numbers. Formally, they are simply Lean variables of type `Nat`.)
144-
145--- Here is a decorated version of this program, embodying a proof of this
146--- specification:
147-
148---   {{ True }} ->>
149---   {{ m = m }}
150---     X := m
151---                        {{ X = m }} ->>
152---                        {{ X = m /\ p = p }};
153---     Z := p;
154---                        {{ X = m /\ Z = p }} ->>
155---                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
156---     while X <> 0 do
157---                        {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
158---                        {{ (Z - 1) - (X - 1) = p - m }}
159---       Z := Z - 1
160---                        {{ Z - (X - 1) = p - m }};
161---       X := X - 1
162---                        {{ Z - X = p - m }}
163---     end
164---   {{ Z - X = p - m /\ ~ (X <> 0) }} ->>
165---   {{ Z = p - m }}
166-

168---     `HIDE: MRC'20: It bothers me a little in the proof above (and
169---     similarly throughout the whole file really when it comes to guards)

171---     [[
172---      while X <> 0 do {{ Z - X = p - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
173---     ]]
174---     we are inconsistent about [X <> 0] vs. [~(X=0)].  I admit they
175---     evaluate the same (er, sort of---the former is a [bexp] whereas the

189-
190--- Concretely, a decorated program consists of the program's text interleaved
191--- with assertions (sometimes multiple assertions separated by ->>).
192-
193--- A decorated program can be viewed as a compact representation of a proof in
194--- Hoare Logic: the assertions surrounding each command specify the Hoare
195--- triple to be proved for that part of the program using one of the Hoare
196--- Logic rules, and the structure of the program itself shows how to assemble
197--- all these individual steps into a proof for the whole program.
198-
199--- Our goal is to verify such decorated programs "mostly automatically." But,
200--- before we can verify anything, we need to be able to *find* a proof for a
201--- given specification, and for this we need to discover the right assertions.
202--- This can be done in an almost mechanical way, with the exception of finding
203--- loop invariants. In the remainder of this section, we explain in detail how
204--- to construct decorations for several short programs, all of which are loop
205--- free or have simple loop invariants. We'll return to finding more
206--- interesting loop invariants later in the chapter.
207-
208--- ### Example: Swapping
209-
210--- Consider the following program, which swaps the values of two variables
211--- using addition and subtraction, instead of by assigning to a temporary
212--- variable.
213-
214---   X := X + Y;
215---   Y := X - Y;
216---   X := X - Y
217-
218--- We can give a proof, in the form of decorations, that this program is
219--- correct — i.e., it really swaps `X` and `Y` — as follows.
220-
221---   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>
222---   (2)    {{ (X + Y) - ((X + Y) - Y) = n /\ (X + Y) - Y = m }}
223---            X := X + Y
224---   (3)                     {{ X - (X - Y) = n /\ X - Y = m }};
225---            Y := X - Y
226---   (4)                     {{ X - Y = n /\ Y = m }};
227---            X := X - Y
228---   (5)    {{ X = n /\ Y = m }}
229-
230--- The decorations can be constructed as follows:
231-
232--- - We begin with the undecorated program (the unnumbered lines).
233-
234--- - We add the specification — i.e., the outer precondition (1) and
235---   postcondition (5). In the precondition, we use parameters `m` and `n` to
236---   remember the initial values of variables `X` and `Y` so that we can refer
237---   to them in the postcondition (5).
238-
239--- - We work backwards, mechanically, starting from (5) and proceeding until we
240---   get to (2). At each step, we obtain the precondition of the assignment from
241---   its postcondition by substituting the assigned variable with the
242---   right-hand-side of the assignment. For instance, we obtain (4) by
243---   substituting `X` with `X - Y` in (5), and we obtain (3) by substituting `Y`
244---   with `X - Y` in (4).
245-
246--- - Finally, we verify that (1) logically implies (2) — i.e., that the step
247---   from (1) to (2) is a valid use of the law of consequence — by doing a bit
248---   of high-school algebra.
249-
250--- Note to developers:
251---     HIDE: BCP 21: This side comment seems too technical:
252---
253---     - (Note that we are working with natural numbers rather than fixed-width
254---       machine integers, so we don't need to worry about the possibility of
255---       arithmetic overflow anywhere in this argument. This makes life quite a
256---       bit simpler!)
257---
258---     HIDE: A quick / optional exercise using just assignment here would be
259---     good.
260-
261--- ### Example: Simple Conditionals
262-
263--- Here is a simple decorated program using conditionals:
264-
265---   (1)   {{ True }}
266---           if X <= Y then
267---   (2)                    {{ True /\ X <= Y }} ->>
268---   (3)                    {{ (Y - X) + X = Y \/ (Y - X) + Y = X }}
269---             Z := Y - X
270---   (4)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
271---           else
272---   (5)                    {{ True /\ ~(X <= Y) }} ->>
273---   (6)                    {{ (X - Y) + X = Y \/ (X - Y) + Y = X }}
274---             Z := X - Y
275---   (7)                    {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
276---           end
277---   (8)   {{ Z + X = Y \/ Z + Y = X }}
278-
279--- These decorations can be constructed as follows:
280-
281--- - We start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (8).
282-
283--- - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_if` rule, we copy the
284---   postcondition (8) to (4) and (7). We conjoin the precondition (1) with the
285---   guard of the conditional to obtain (2). We conjoin (1) with the negated
286---   guard of the conditional to obtain (5).
287-
288--- - In order to use the assignment rule and obtain (3), we substitute `Z` by
289---   `Y - X` in (4). To obtain (6) we substitute `Z` by `X - Y` in (7).
290-
291--- - Finally, we verify that (2) implies (3) and (5) implies (6). Both of these
292---   implications crucially depend on the ordering of `X` and `Y` obtained from
293---   the guard. For instance, knowing that `X <= Y` ensures that subtracting `X`
294---   from `Y` and then adding back `X` produces `Y`, as required by the first
295---   disjunct of (3). Similarly, knowing that `~ (X <= Y)` ensures that
296---   subtracting `Y` from `X` and then adding back `Y` produces `X`, as needed
297---   by the second disjunct of (6). Note that `n - m + m = n` does *not* hold
298---   for arbitrary natural numbers `n` and `m` (for example, [3 - 5 + 5 = 5]).
299-
300--- Note to developers:
301---     NOTATION: LATER: The `~` in that paragraph will typeset wrong if the
302---     space after it is removed. Maybe it's better to give up on all the
303---     unicode hacks in the generated HTML...?

305--- ### Exercise (2 stars): if_minus_plus_reloaded (manually graded) ⭐⭐
306-
307--- N.b.: Although this exercise is marked optional, it is an excellent warm-up
308--- for the (non-optional) `if_minus_plus_correct` exercise below!
309-
310--- Fill in valid decorations for the following program:
311-
312---   {{ True }}
313---     if X <= Y then
314---               {{                         }} ->>
315---               {{                         }}
316---       Z := Y - X
317---               {{                         }}
318---     else
319---               {{                         }} ->>
320---               {{                         }}
321---       Y := X + Z
322---               {{                         }}
323---     end
324---   {{ Y = X + Z }}
325-
326--- Briefly justify each use of `->>`.
327-
328---   {{ True }}
329---     if X <= Y then
330---          {{ True /\ X <= Y }} ->>
331---          {{ Y = X + (Y - X) }}
332---       Z := Y - X
333---          {{ Y = X + Z }}
334---     else
335---          {{ True /\ ~(X <= Y) }} ->>
336---          {{ X + Z = X + Z }}
337---       Y := X + Z
338---          {{ Y = X + Z }}
339---     end
340---   {{ Y = X + Z }}
341-
342--- The second use of consequence is trivial, while the first crucially depends
343--- on the `X <= Y` condition, which ensures that subtracting `X` from `Y` and
344--- then adding back `X` produces `Y`.
345-
346--- ### Example: Reduce to Zero
347-
348--- Here is a `while` loop that is so simple that `True` suffices as a loop
349--- invariant.
350-
351---   (1)    {{ True }}
352---            while X <> 0 do
353---   (2)                  {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>
354---   (3)                  {{ True }}
355---              X := X - 1
356---   (4)                  {{ True }}
357---            end
358---   (5)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>
359---   (6)    {{ X = 0 }}
360-
361--- The decorations can be constructed as follows:
362-
363--- - Start with the outer precondition (1) and postcondition (6).
364-
365--- - Following the format dictated by the `hoare_while` rule, we copy (1) to
366---   (4). We conjoin (1) with the guard to obtain (2). We also conjoin (1) with
367---   the negation of the guard to obtain (5).
368-
369--- - Because the final postcondition (6) does not syntactically match (5), we
370---   add an implication between them.
371-
372--- - Using the assignment rule with assertion (4), we trivially substitute and
373---   obtain assertion (3).
374-
375--- - We add the implication between (2) and (3).
376-
377--- Finally we check that the implications do hold; both are trivial.
378-
379--- ### Example: Division
380-
381--- Let's do one more example of simple reasoning about a loop.
382-
383--- The following Imp program calculates the integer quotient and remainder of
384--- parameters `m` and `n`.
385-
386---   X := m;
387---   Y := 0;
388---   while n <= X do
389---     X := X - n;
390---     Y := Y + 1
391---   end;
392-
393--- If we replace `m` and `n` by concrete numbers and execute the program, it
394--- will terminate with the variable `X` set to the remainder when `m` is
395--- divided by `n` and `Y` set to the quotient.
396-
397--- In order to give a specification to this program we need to remember that
398--- dividing `m` by `n` produces a remainder `X` and a quotient `Y` such that
399--- `n * Y + X = m /\ X < n`.
400-
401--- It turns out that we get lucky with this program and don't have to think
402--- very hard about the loop invariant: the loop invariant is just the first
403--- conjunct, `n * Y + X = m`, and we can use this to decorate the program.
404-
405---    (1)  {{ True }} ->>
406---    (2)  {{ n * 0 + m = m }}
407---           X := m;
408---    (3)                     {{ n * 0 + X = m }}
409---           Y := 0;
410---    (4)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
411---           while n <= X do
412---    (5)                     {{ n * Y + X = m /\ n <= X }} ->>
413---    (6)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + (X - n) = m }}
414---             X := X - n;
415---    (7)                     {{ n * (Y + 1) + X = m }}
416---             Y := Y + 1
417---    (8)                     {{ n * Y + X = m }}
418---           end
419---    (9)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ ~ (n <= X) }} ->>
420---   (10)  {{ n * Y + X = m /\ X < n }}
421-
422--- Assertions (4), (5), (8), and (9) are derived mechanically from the loop
423--- invariant and the loop's guard. Assertions (8), (7), and (6) are derived
424--- using the assignment rule going backwards from (8) to (6). Assertions (4),
425--- (3), and (2) are again backwards applications of the assignment rule.
426-
427--- Now that we've decorated the program it only remains to check that the uses
428--- of the consequence rule are correct — i.e., that (1) implies (2), that (5)
429--- implies (6), and that (9) implies (10). This is indeed the case:
430-
431--- - (1) ->> (2): trivial, by algebra.
432-
433--- - (5) ->> (6): because `n <= X`, we are guaranteed that the subtraction in
434---   (6) does not get zero-truncated. We can therefore rewrite (6) as
435---   `n * Y + n + X - n` and cancel the `n`s, which results in the left conjunct
436---   of (5).
437-
438--- - (9) ->> (10): if `~ (n <= X)` then `X < n`. That's straightforward from
439---   high-school algebra. So, we have a valid decorated program.
440-
441--- ### From Decorated Programs to Formal Proofs
442-
443--- From an informal proof in the form of a decorated program, it is "easy in
444--- principle" to read off a formal proof using the Lean theorems corresponding
445--- to the Hoare Logic rules, but these proofs can be a bit long and fiddly.
446-
447--- Note that we do *not* unfold the definition of `ValidHoareTriple` anywhere
448--- in this proof: the point of the game we're playing now is to use the Hoare
449--- rules as a self-contained logic for reasoning about programs.
450-
451--- For example...
452-
453-def reduceToZero : Com :=
454-  imp {
455-    while (X ≠ 0) {
456-      X := X - 1
457-    }
458-  }
459-
460-theorem reduce_to_zero_correct' :
461-    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
462-  -- First put the postcondition into the form expected by
463-  -- the while rule.
464-  sorry
465-
466--- In Hoare we introduced a series of tactics named `assertion_auto` to
467--- automate proofs involving assertions.
468-
469--- The following declaration introduces a more sophisticated tactic that will
470--- help with proving assertions throughout the rest of this chapter. You don't
471--- need to understand the details, but briefly: it introduces the available
472--- hypotheses, simplifies assertions, maps, and arithmetic expressions, and
473--- then asks `lia` to solve linear arithmetic goals. What's left after
474--- `verify_assertion` does its work should be just the "interesting parts" of
475--- the proof (which, if we're lucky, might be nothing at all!).
476-
477-macro "verify_assertion" : tactic =>
478-  `(tactic| assertion_auto)
479-
480--- This makes it pretty easy to verify `reduce_to_zero`:
481-
482-theorem reduce_to_zero_correct''' :
483-    {{ True }} ~reduceToZero {{ X = 0 }} := by
484-  sorry
485-
486--- This example shows that it is conceptually straightforward to read off the
487--- main elements of a formal proof from a decorated program. Indeed, the
488--- process is so straightforward that it can be automated, as we will see
489--- next.
490-
491--- ## Formal Decorated Programs
492-
493--- Our informal conventions for decorated programs amount to a way of
494--- "displaying" Hoare triples, in which commands are annotated with enough
495--- embedded assertions that checking the validity of a triple is reduced to
496--- simple logical and algebraic calculations showing that some assertions
497--- imply others.
498-
499--- In this section, we show that this presentation style can be made
500--- completely formal — and indeed that checking the validity of decorated
501--- programs can be largely automated.
502-
503--- ### Syntax
504-
505--- The first thing we need to do is to formalize a variant of the syntax of
506--- Imp commands that includes embedded assertions, which we'll call
507--- "decorations." We call the new commands *decorated commands*, or `dcom`s.
508-
509--- The choice of exactly where to put assertions in the definition of `dcom`
510--- is a bit subtle. The simplest thing to do would be to annotate every `dcom`
511--- with a precondition and postcondition — something like this...
512-
513-namespace DComFirstTry
514-
515-inductive DCom where
516-  | skip (pre : Assertion)
517-  | seq (pre : Assertion) (first : DCom)
518-      (middle : Assertion)
519-      (second : DCom) (post : Assertion)
520-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
521-  | cond (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
522-      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
523-      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
524-      (post : Assertion)
525-  | whileDo (pre : Assertion) (b : Bexp)
526-      (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
527-      (bodyPost : Assertion) (post : Assertion)
528-  | strengthenPre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
529-  | weakenPost (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
530-
531-end DComFirstTry
532-
533--- But this would result in *very* verbose decorated programs with a lot of
534--- repeated annotations: a simple program like `skip;skip` would be decorated
535--- like this,
536-
537---   {{P}} ({{P}} skip {{P}}) ; ({{P}} skip {{P}}) {{P}}
538-
539--- with pre- and post-conditions around each `skip`, plus identical pre- and
540--- post-conditions on the semicolon!
541-
542--- In other words, we don't want both preconditions and postconditions on each
543--- command, because a sequence of two commands would contain redundant
544--- decorations — the postcondition of the first likely being the same as the
545--- precondition of the second.
546-
547--- Instead, our formal syntax of decorated commands will omit preconditions
548--- whenever possible and embed just postconditions.
549-
550--- - The `skip` command, for example, is decorated only with its postcondition
551-
552---   skip {{ Q }}
553-
554--- on the assumption that the precondition will be provided by somebody else.
555-
556--- We carry the same assumption through the other syntactic forms: each
557--- decorated command is assumed to carry its own postcondition within itself
558--- but take its precondition from its context in which it is used.
559-
560--- - Sequences `d1 ; d2` need no additional decorations.
561-
562--- Why?
563-
564--- Because inside `d2` there will be a postcondition, which also serves as the
565--- postcondition of `d1;d2`.
566-
567--- Similarly, inside `d1` there will also be a postcondition, which
568--- additionally serves as the *precondition* for `d2`.
569-
570--- - An assignment `X := a` is decorated only with its postcondition:
571-
572---   X := a {{ Q }}
573-
574--- - A conditional `if b then d1 else d2` is decorated with a postcondition for
575---   the entire statement, as well as preconditions for each branch:
576-
577---   if b then {{ P1 }} d1 else {{ P2 }} d2 end {{ Q }}
578-
579--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
580---     Maybe we need a note here about why we don't just calculate P1 and P2
581---     later, once we know the precondition of the whole loop. Indeed, we
582---     could (and perhaps should, as discussed elsewhere), but we are doing
583---     something simpler for the moment.
584-
585--- - A loop `while b do d end` is decorated with its final postcondition plus a
586---   precondition for the body:
587-
588---   while b do {{ P }} d end {{ Q }}
589-
590--- The postcondition embedded in `d` serves as the loop invariant.
591-
592--- - Implications `->>` can be added as decorations either for a precondition...
593-
594---   ->> {{ P }} d
595-
596--- ...or for a postcondition:
597-
598---   d ->> {{ Q }}
599-
600--- The former is waiting for another precondition to be supplied by the
601--- context; the latter relies on the postcondition already embedded in `d`.
602-
603--- Putting this all together gives us the formal syntax of decorated commands:
604-
605-inductive DCom where
606-  | skip (post : Assertion)
607-  | seq (first second : DCom)
608-  | asgn (x : Ident) (a : Aexp) (post : Assertion)
609-  | cond (b : Bexp)
610-      (thenPre : Assertion) (thenBranch : DCom)
611-      (elsePre : Assertion) (elseBranch : DCom)
612-      (post : Assertion)
613-  | whileDo (b : Bexp) (bodyPre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
614-      (post : Assertion)
615-  | pre (pre : Assertion) (body : DCom)
616-  | post (body : DCom) (post : Assertion)
617-
618--- Lean keeps decorated-command notation in its own syntax category, `dcom`,
619--- so it can coexist with the ordinary Imp command syntax.
620-
621--- THESE DETAILS CAN BE SKIPPED: Notation encoding: decorated commands
622-
623-declare_syntax_cat dcom
624-
625-syntax:max "(" dcom ")" : dcom
626-syntax:max "skip" " {{" term "}}" : dcom
627-syntax:max ident " := " imp_aexp " {{" term "}}" : dcom
628-syntax:20 dcom:21 ";" ppLine dcom:20 : dcom
629-syntax:max "if " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "then" ppLine
630-  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
631-  "else" ppLine "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
632-  "end" ppLine "{{" term "}}" : dcom
633-syntax:max "while " "(" imp_bexp ")" ppHardSpace "do" ppLine
634-  "{{" term "}}" ppLine dcom ppLine
635-  "end" ppLine "{{" term "}}" : dcom
636-syntax:5 "->>" " {{" term "}}" ppLine dcom:0 : dcom
637-syntax:5 dcom:6 ppLine "->>" " {{" term "}}" : dcom
638-
639-syntax:min "dcom" ppHardSpace "{" ppLine dcom
640-  ppDedent(ppLine "}") : term
641-
642-macro_rules
643-  | `(dcom { ($body:dcom) }) =>
644-      `(dcom { $body })
645-  | `(dcom { skip {{ $q }} }) =>
646-      `(DCom.skip ({{ $q }}))
647-  | `(dcom { $x:ident := $a:imp_aexp {{ $q }} }) =>
648-      `(DCom.asgn $x (aexp { $a }) ({{ $q }}))
649-  | `(dcom { $d1:dcom; $d2:dcom }) =>
650-      `(DCom.seq (dcom { $d1 }) (dcom { $d2 }))
651-  | `(dcom {
652-        if ($b:imp_bexp) then
653-          {{ $p1 }}
654-          $d1:dcom
655-        else
656-          {{ $p2 }}
657-          $d2:dcom
658-        end
659-          {{ $q }}
660-      }) =>
661-      `(DCom.cond (bexp { $b })
662-        ({{ $p1 }}) (dcom { $d1 })
663-        ({{ $p2 }}) (dcom { $d2 })
664-        ({{ $q }}))
665-  | `(dcom {
666-        while ($b:imp_bexp) do
667-          {{ $p }}
668-          $body:dcom
669-        end
670-          {{ $q }}
671-      }) =>
672-      `(DCom.whileDo (bexp { $b }) ({{ $p }})
673-        (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
674-  | `(dcom { ->> {{ $p }} $body:dcom }) =>
675-      `(DCom.pre ({{ $p }}) (dcom { $body }))
676-  | `(dcom { $body:dcom ->> {{ $q }} }) =>
677-      `(DCom.post (dcom { $body }) ({{ $q }}))
678-
679--- END DETAILS
680-
681--- To provide the initial precondition that goes at the very top of a
682--- decorated program, we introduce a new type `decorated`:
683-
684-structure Decorated where
685-  pre : Assertion
686-  body : DCom
687-

689---     HIDE: Add FOLD here

691-example : DCom :=
692-  .skip ({{ True }})

695-  .whileDo (bexp {true}) ({{ True }})

698--- To inspect the fully elaborated term behind this notation, put
699--- `set_option pp.all true in` before a `#check` or `#print` command.
700-
701--- The formal definitions can use either constructors directly or the
702--- decorated-command notation introduced above.
703-
704--- Note to developers:
705---     HIDE: Add /FOLD here
706-
707--- An example `decorated` program that decrements `X` to `0`:
708-
709-def decWhile : Decorated where
710-  pre := ({{ True }})
711-  body := dcom {
712-    while (X ≠ 0) do
713-      {{ True ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
714-      X := X - 1 {{ True }}
715-    end
716-      {{ True ∧ X = 0 }}
717-    ->> {{ X = 0 }}
718-  }
719-
720--- It is easy to go from a `dcom` to a `com` by erasing all annotations.
721-
722-def DCom.erase (d : DCom) : Com :=
723-  match d with
724-  | .skip _ => .skip
725-  | .seq d1 d2 => .seq d1.erase d2.erase
726-  | .asgn x a _ => .asgn x a
727-  | .cond b _ d1 _ d2 _ => .cond b d1.erase d2.erase
728-  | .whileDo b _ body _ => .whileDo b body.erase
729-  | .pre _ body => body.erase
730-  | .post body _ => body.erase
731-
732-def Decorated.erase (dec : Decorated) : Com :=
733-  dec.body.erase
734-
735-example :

745--- from a decorated program.
746-
747-def Decorated.precondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
748-  dec.pre

750--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00, before next release, 2025):
751---     `It would be nice to use <{ ... }> notations
752---     in this definition and the ones below...
753---          | <{ skip {{P}} }>        => P
754---          | <{ _; d2 }>             => post d2
755---          | <{ _ := _ {{Q}} }>      => Q`

757-def DCom.postcondition (d : DCom) : Assertion :=
758-  match d with
759-  | .skip q => q
760-  | .seq _ d2 => d2.postcondition
761-  | .asgn _ _ q => q
762-  | .cond _ _ _ _ _ q => q
763-  | .whileDo _ _ _ q => q
764-  | .pre _ body => body.postcondition
765-  | .post _ q => q
766-
767-def Decorated.postcondition (dec : Decorated) : Assertion :=
768-  dec.body.postcondition
769-
770-example : decWhile.precondition = {{ True }} := by

772-  rfl

778--- We can then express what it means for a decorated program to be correct as
779--- follows:
780-
781-def Decorated.OuterTripleValid (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
782-  ValidHoareTriple dec.precondition dec.erase
783-    dec.postcondition
784-
785--- For example:
786-
787-example :
788-    decWhile.OuterTripleValid =
789-      {{ True }}
790-        while (X ≠ 0) {
791-          X := X - 1
792-        }
793-      {{ X = 0 }} := by
794-  rfl
795-
796--- The outer Hoare triple of a decorated program is just a `Prop`; thus, to
797--- show that it is *valid*, we need to produce a proof of this proposition.
798-
799--- We will do this by extracting "proof obligations" from the decorations
800--- sprinkled throughout the program.
801-
802--- These obligations are often called *verification conditions*, because they
803--- are the facts that must be verified to see that the decorations are locally
804--- consistent and thus constitute a proof of validity of the outer triple.
805-
806--- ### Extracting Verification Conditions
807-
808--- The function `DCom.VerificationConditions` takes a decorated command `d`
809--- together with a precondition `P` and returns a *proposition* that, if it
810--- can be proved, implies that the triple
811-
812---   {{P}} d.erase {{d.postcondition}}
813-
814--- is valid.
815-
816--- It does this by walking over `d` and generating a big conjunction that
817--- includes
818-
819--- - local consistency checks for each form of command, plus
820-
821--- - uses of `->>` to bridge the gap between the assertions found inside a
822---   decorated command and the assertions imposed by the external precondition;
823---   these uses correspond to applications of the consequence rule.
824-
825--- *Local consistency* is defined as follows...
826-
827--- - The decorated command
828-
829---   skip {{Q}}
830-
831--- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if `P ->> Q`.
832-
833--- - The sequential composition of `d1` and `d2` is locally consistent with
834---   respect to `P` if `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P` and `d2`
835---   is locally consistent with respect to the postcondition of `d1`.
836-
837--- - An assignment
838-
839---   X := a {{Q}}
840-
841--- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
842-
843---   P ->> Q [X |-> a]
844-
845--- - A conditional
846-
847---   if b then {{P1}} d1 else {{P2}} d2 end {{Q}}
848-
849--- is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if
850-
851--- (1) `P /\ b ->> P1`
852-
853--- (2) `P /\ ~b ->> P2`
854-
855--- (3) `d1` is locally consistent with respect to `P1`
856-
857--- (4) `d2` is locally consistent with respect to `P2`
858-
859--- (5) `d1.postcondition ->> Q`
860-
861--- (6) `d2.postcondition ->> Q`
862-
863--- - A loop
864-
865---   while b do {{Q}} d end {{R}}
866-
867--- is locally consistent with respect to precondition `P` if:
868-
869--- (1) `P ->> d.postcondition`
870-
871--- (2) `d.postcondition /\ b ->> Q`
872-
873--- (3) `d.postcondition /\ ~b ->> R`
874-
875--- (4) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
876-
877--- - A command with an extra assertion at the beginning
878-
879---   ->> {{Q}} d
880-
881--- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
882-
883--- (1) `P ->> Q`
884-
885--- (2) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `Q`
886-
887--- - A command with an extra assertion at the end
888-
889---   d ->> {{Q}}
890-
891--- is locally consistent with respect to a precondition `P` if:
892-
893--- (1) `d` is locally consistent with respect to `P`
894-
895--- (2) `d.postcondition ->> Q`
896-
897--- With all this in mind, we can write a *verification condition generator*
898--- that takes a decorated command and reads off a proposition saying that all
899--- its decorations are locally consistent.
900-
901--- Formally, since a decorated command is "waiting for its precondition" the
902--- main VC generator takes a `dcom` plus a given precondition as arguments.
903-
904--- Note to developers:
905---     HIDE: There was some discussion in 2016 about whether the VC generator
906---     should should use equivalence or implication in a few places. I (BCP)
907---     believe Phil (Wadler) changed some instances of the former to the
908---     latter.
909---
910---     HIDE: MRC'20: a written explanation of each part of this would be quite
911---     nice. BCP 21: Agreed!! (BCP 23: But it's kind of what's just above...)
912-
913-def DCom.VerificationConditions
914-    (P : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
915-  match d with
916-  | .skip Q =>
917-      P ->> Q
918-  | .seq d1 d2 =>
919-      d1.VerificationConditions P ∧
920-      d2.VerificationConditions d1.postcondition
921-  | .asgn x a Q =>
922-      P ->> {{ Q [x ↦ ~a] }}
923-  | .cond b P1 d1 P2 d2 Q =>
924-      ({{ P ∧ b }} ->> P1) ∧
925-      ({{ P ∧ ¬ b }} ->> P2) ∧
926-      (d1.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
927-      (d2.postcondition ->> Q) ∧
928-      d1.VerificationConditions P1 ∧
929-      d2.VerificationConditions P2
930-  | .whileDo b bodyPre body q =>
931-      -- The body's postcondition is both the loop invariant
932-      -- and the precondition for the first iteration.
933-      (P ->> body.postcondition) ∧
934-      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ b }} ->> bodyPre) ∧
935-      ({{ body.postcondition ∧ ¬ b }} ->> q) ∧
936-      body.VerificationConditions bodyPre
937-  | .pre P' body =>
938-      (P ->> P') ∧ body.VerificationConditions P'
939-  | .post body Q =>
940-      body.VerificationConditions P ∧
941-      (body.postcondition ->> Q)
942-
943--- The following key theorem states that `DCom.VerificationConditions` does
944--- its job correctly. Not surprisingly, each of the Hoare Logic rules plays a
945--- critical role at some point in the proof.
946-
947-theorem verification_correct (d : DCom) (P : Assertion)
948-    (hvc : d.VerificationConditions P) :
949-    ValidHoareTriple P d.erase d.postcondition := by
950-  sorry
951-
952--- Now that all the pieces are in place, we can define what it means to verify
953--- an entire program.
954-
955-def Decorated.VerificationConditions
956-    (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
957-  dec.body.VerificationConditions dec.pre
958-
959--- And this brings us to the main theorem of this section:
960-
961-theorem verification_conditions_correct (dec : Decorated)
962-    (hvc : dec.VerificationConditions) :
963-    dec.OuterTripleValid := by
964-  exact verification_correct dec.body dec.pre hvc
965-
966--- ### More Automation
967-
968--- The propositions generated by `DCom.VerificationConditions` are fairly big
969--- and contain many conjuncts that are essentially trivial.
970-
971--- Note to developers:
972---     `HIDE: MRC'20: The conditions here used to be just [Eval]ed instead
973---     of being duplicated in a comment.  They were actually incorrect
974---     because of changes to notation.  Putting them in as an [Example]
975---     will force us to keep them up-to-date. APT20: Yes, but but stating
976---     this an equality completely misses the point about verify_assertion! So I
977---     changed things back.`
978-
979-example : decWhile.VerificationConditions := by
980-  unfold Decorated.VerificationConditions decWhile
981-  simp only [DCom.VerificationConditions,
982-    DCom.postcondition]
983-  sorry
984-
985--- Fortunately, our `verify_assertion` tactic can generally take care of most
986--- (or sometimes all) of them.
987-
988-example : decWhile.VerificationConditions := by
989-  sorry
990-
991--- To automate the overall process of verification, we can use
992--- `verification_correct` to extract the verification conditions, use
993--- `verify_assertion` to verify them as much as it can, and finally tidy up
994--- any remaining bits by hand.
995-
996-macro "verify" : tactic =>
997-  `(tactic|
998-    (apply verification_conditions_correct;
999-     verify_assertion))
1000-

1094-
1095--- ## Finding Loop Invariants
1096-
1097--- Once the outermost precondition and postcondition are chosen, the only
1098--- creative part of a verifying program using Hoare Logic is finding the right
1099--- loop invariants. The reason this is difficult is the same as the reason
1100--- that inductive mathematical proofs are:
1101-
1102--- - Strengthening a *loop invariant* means that you have a stronger assumption
1103---   to work with when trying to establish the postcondition of the loop body,
1104---   but it also means that the loop body's postcondition is harder to prove.
1105-
1106--- - Similarly, strengthening an *induction hypothesis* means that you have a
1107---   stronger assumption to work with when trying to complete the induction step
1108---   of the proof, but it also means that the statement being proved inductively
1109---   is harder to prove.
1110-
1111--- This section explains how to approach the challenge of finding loop
1112--- invariants through a series of examples and exercises.
1113-
1114--- ### Example: Slow Subtraction
1115-
1116--- The following program subtracts the value of `X` from the value of `Y` by
1117--- repeatedly decrementing both `X` and `Y`. We want to verify its correctness
1118--- with respect to the pre- and postconditions shown:
1119-
1120---   {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}
1121---     while X <> 0 do
1122---       Y := Y - 1;
1123---       X := X - 1
1124---     end
1125---   {{ Y = n - m }}
1126-
1127--- To verify this program, we need to find an invariant `Inv` for the loop. As
1128--- a first step we can leave `Inv` as an unknown and build a *skeleton* for
1129--- the proof by applying the rules for local consistency, working from the end
1130--- of the program to the beginning, as usual, and without doing any thinking
1131--- at all yet.
1132-
1133--- This leads to the following skeleton:
1134-
1135---   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }}  ->>                   (a)
1136---   (2)    {{ Inv }}
1137---            while X <> 0 do
1138---   (3)              {{ Inv /\ X <> 0 }}  ->>          (c)
1139---   (4)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] [Y |-> Y-1] }}
1140---              Y := Y - 1;
1141---   (5)              {{ Inv [X |-> X-1] }}
1142---              X := X - 1
1143---   (6)              {{ Inv }}
1144---            end
1145---   (7)    {{ Inv /\ ~ (X <> 0) }}  ->>                (b)
1146---   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1147-
1148--- Examining this skeleton, we can see that any valid `Inv` will have to
1149--- respect three conditions:
1150-
1151--- - (a) it must be *weak* enough to be implied by the loop's precondition,
1152---   i.e., (1) must imply (2);
1153-
1154--- - (b) it must be *strong* enough to imply the program's postcondition, i.e.,
1155---   (7) must imply (8);
1156-
1157--- - (c) it must be *preserved* by a single iteration of the loop, assuming that
1158---   the loop guard also evaluates to true, i.e., (3) must imply (4).
1159-
1160--- These conditions are actually independent of the particular program and
1161--- specification we are considering: every loop invariant has to satisfy them.
1162-
1163--- One way to find a loop invariant that simultaneously satisfies these three
1164--- conditions is by using an iterative process: start with a "candidate"
1165--- invariant (e.g., a guess or a heuristic choice) and check the three
1166--- conditions above; if any of the checks fails, try to use the information
1167--- that we get from the failure to produce another — hopefully better —
1168--- candidate invariant, and repeat.
1169-
1170--- For instance, in the reduce-to-zero example above, we saw that, for a very
1171--- simple loop, choosing `True` as a loop invariant did the job. Maybe it will
1172--- work here too. To find out, let's try instantiating `Inv` with `True` in
1173--- the skeleton above and see what we get...
1174-
1175---   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                    (a - OK)
1176---   (2)    {{ True }}
1177---            while X <> 0 do
1178---   (3)                   {{ True /\ X <> 0 }} ->>     (c - OK)
1179---   (4)                   {{ True }}
1180---              Y := Y - 1;
1181---   (5)                   {{ True }}
1182---              X := X - 1
1183---   (6)                   {{ True }}
1184---            end
1185---   (7)    {{ True /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                 (b - WRONG!)
1186---   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1187-
1188--- While conditions (a) and (c) are trivially satisfied, (b) is wrong: it is
1189--- not the case that `True /\ X = 0` (7) implies `Y = n - m` (8). In fact, the
1190--- two assertions are completely unrelated, so it is very easy to find a
1191--- counterexample to the implication (say, `Y = X = m = 0` and `n = 1`).
1192-
1193--- If we want (b) to hold, we need to strengthen the loop invariant so that it
1194--- implies the postcondition (8). One simple way to do this is to let the loop
1195--- invariant *be* the postcondition. So let's return to our skeleton,
1196--- instantiate `Inv` with `Y = n - m`, and try checking conditions (a) to (c)
1197--- again.
1198-
1199---   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                        (a - WRONG!)
1200---   (2)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1201---            while X <> 0 do
1202---   (3)                     {{ Y = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>  (c - WRONG!)
1203---   (4)                     {{ Y - 1 = n - m }}
1204---              Y := Y - 1;
1205---   (5)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1206---              X := X - 1
1207---   (6)                     {{ Y = n - m }}
1208---            end
1209---   (7)    {{ Y = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1210---   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1211-
1212--- This time, condition (b) holds trivially, but (a) and (c) are broken.
1213--- Condition (a) requires that (1) `X = m /\ Y = n` implies (2) `Y = n - m`.
1214--- If we substitute `Y` by `n` we have to show that `n = n - m` for arbitrary
1215--- `m` and `n`, which is not the case (for instance, when `m = n = 1`).
1216--- Condition (c) requires that `n - m - 1 = n - m`, which fails, for instance,
1217--- for `n = 1` and `m = 0`. So, although `Y = n - m` holds at the end of the
1218--- loop, it does not hold from the start, and it doesn't hold on each
1219--- iteration; it is not a correct loop invariant.
1220-
1221--- This failure is not very surprising: the variable `Y` changes during the
1222--- loop, while `m` and `n` are constant, so the assertion we chose didn't have
1223--- much chance of being a loop invariant!
1224-
1225--- To do better, we need to generalize (7) to some statement that is
1226--- equivalent to (8) when `X` is `0`, since this will be the case when the
1227--- loop terminates, and that "fills the gap" in some appropriate way when `X`
1228--- is nonzero. Looking at how the loop works, we can observe that `X` and `Y`
1229--- are decremented together until `X` reaches `0`. So, if `X = 2` and `Y = 5`
1230--- initially, after one iteration of the loop we obtain `X = 1` and `Y = 4`;
1231--- after two iterations `X = 0` and `Y = 3`; and then the loop stops. Notice
1232--- that the difference between `Y` and `X` stays constant between iterations:
1233--- initially, `Y = n` and `X = m`, and the difference is always `n - m`. So
1234--- let's try instantiating `Inv` in the skeleton above with `Y - X = n - m`.
1235-
1236---   (1)    {{ X = m /\ Y = n }} ->>                            (a - OK)
1237---   (2)    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1238---            while X <> 0 do
1239---   (3)                    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ X <> 0 }} ->>   (c - OK)
1240---   (4)                    {{ (Y - 1) - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1241---              Y := Y - 1;
1242---   (5)                    {{ Y - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1243---              X := X - 1
1244---   (6)                    {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1245---            end
1246---   (7)    {{ Y - X = n - m /\ ~(X <> 0) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1247---   (8)    {{ Y = n - m }}
1248-
1249--- Success! Conditions (a), (b) and (c) all hold now. (To verify (c), we need
1250--- to check that, under the assumption that `X <> 0`, we have
1251--- `Y - X = (Y - 1) - (X - 1)`; this holds for all natural numbers `X` and
1252--- `Y`.)
1253-
1254--- Here is the final version of the decorated program:
1255-
1256-def subtractSlowlyDec (m n : Nat) : Decorated where
1257-  pre := ({{ X = m ∧ Y = n }})
1258-  body := dcom {
1259-    ->> {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1260-    while (X ≠ 0) do
1261-      {{ Y - X = n - m ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}
1262-      ->> {{ (Y - 1) - (X - 1) = n - m }}
1263-      Y := Y - 1 {{ Y - (X - 1) = n - m }};
1264-      X := X - 1 {{ Y - X = n - m }}
1265-    end
1266-      {{ Y - X = n - m ∧ X = 0 }}
1267-    ->> {{ Y = n - m }}
1268-  }
1269-
1270-theorem subtract_slowly_outer_triple_valid (m n : Nat) :
1271-    (subtractSlowlyDec m n).OuterTripleValid := by
1272-  sorry
1273-
1274--- ### Exercise: Slow Assignment
1275-
1276--- ### Exercise (2 stars): slow_assignment ⭐⭐
1277-
1278--- A roundabout way of assigning a number currently stored in `X` to the
1279--- variable `Y` is to start `Y` at `0`, then decrement `X` until it hits `0`,
1280--- incrementing `Y` at each step. Here is a program that implements this idea.
1281--- Fill in decorations and prove the decorated program correct. (The proof
1282--- should be very simple.)
1283-
1284-def slowAssignmentDec (m : Nat) : Decorated where
1285-  pre := ({{ X = m }})
1286-  body := dcom {
1287-    Y := 0 {{ ({{ X = m ∧ Y = 0 }}) }};
1288-    (->> {{ ({{ Y + X = m }}) }}
1289-      while (X ≠ 0) do
1290-        {{ ({{ Y + X = m ∧ ¬ X = 0 }}) }}
1291-        ->> {{ ({{ Y + (X - 1) + 1 = m }}) }}
1292-        X := X - 1 {{ ({{ Y + X + 1 = m }}) }};
1293-        (->> {{ ({{ Y + X + 1 = m }}) }}
1294-          Y := Y + 1 {{ ({{ Y + X = m }}) }})
1295-      end
1296-        {{ ({{ Y + X = m ∧ X = 0 }}) }}
1297-      ->> {{ Y = m }})
1298-  }
1299-
1300-theorem slow_assignment (m : Nat) :
1301-    (slowAssignmentDec m).OuterTripleValid := by
1302-  sorry
1303-
1304--- ### Example: Parity
1305-
1306--- Here is a cute way of computing the parity of a value initially stored in
1307--- `X`, due to Daniel Cristofani.
1308-
1309---   {{ X = m }}
1310---     while 2 <= X do
1311---       X := X - 2
1312---     end
1313---   {{ X = parity m }}
1314-
1315--- The `parity` function used in the specification is defined in Lean as
1316--- follows:
1317-
1318-def parity : Nat → Nat
1319-  | 0 => 0
1320-  | 1 => 1
1321-  | Nat.succ (Nat.succ n) => parity n
1322-
1323--- The postcondition does not hold at the beginning of the loop, since
1324--- `m = parity m` does not hold for an arbitrary `m`, so we cannot hope to use
1325--- that as a loop invariant. To find a loop invariant that works, let's think
1326--- a bit about what this loop does. On each iteration it decrements `X` by
1327--- `2`, which preserves the parity of `X`. So the parity of `X` does not
1328--- change, i.e., it is invariant. The initial value of `X` is `m`, so the
1329--- parity of `X` is always equal to the parity of `m`. Using
1330--- `parity X = parity m` as an invariant we obtain the following decorated
1331--- program:
1332-
1333---   {{ X = m }} ->>                                         (a - OK)
1334---   {{ parity X = parity m }}
1335---     while 2 <= X do
1336---                  {{ parity X = parity m /\ 2 <= X }} ->>  (c - OK)
1337---                  {{ parity (X-2) = parity m }}
1338---       X := X - 2
1339---                  {{ parity X = parity m }}
1340---     end
1341---   {{ parity X = parity m /\ ~(2 <= X) }} ->>              (b - OK)
1342---   {{ X = parity m }}
1343-
1344--- With this loop invariant, conditions (a), (b), and (c) are all satisfied.
1345--- For verifying (b), we observe that, when `X < 2`, we have `parity X = X`
1346--- (we can easily see this in the definition of `parity`). For verifying (c),
1347--- we observe that, when `2 <= X`, we have `parity X = parity (X-2)`.
1348-
1349--- Note to developers:
1350---     `HIDE: A more complexly phrased loop invariant for the same program
1351---     [[
1352---             {{ X = m }}  ->>                        (a - OK)
1353---             {{ ev X <-> ev m }}
1354---           while 2 <= X do
1355---               {{ ev X <-> ev m /\ 2 <= X }}  ->>    (c - OK)
1356---               {{ ev (X-2) <-> ev m }}
1357---             X := X - 2
1358---               {{ ev X <-> ev m }}
1359---           end
1360---             {{ (ev X <-> ev m) /\ ~(2 <= X) }}  ->>     (b - OK)
1361---             {{ X=0 <-> ev m }}
1362---     ]]`
1363---
1364---     `HIDE: find_parity'_dec; more complicated phrasing of invariant
1365---     there is very little resemblance between the invariant and the
1366---     postcondition -- the implication is also non-obvious, and the
1367---     X <= m condition makes the invariant more complicated
1368---     [[
1369---      {{ X = m }} ->>
1370---      {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) }}
1371---     while 2 <= X do
1372---        {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) /\ 2 <= X }} ->>
1373---        {{ X - 2 <= m /\ ev (m - (X - 2)) }}
1374---      X := X - 2
1375---        {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) }}
1376---     end
1377---      {{ X <= m /\ ev (m - X) /\ ~(2 <= X) }} ->>
1378---      {{ X=0 <-> ev m }}
1379---     ]]`

1528-

1530--- iteration:
1531-
1532---   {{ X=m }}
1533---     Z := 0;
1534---     while (Z+1)*(Z+1) <= X do
1535---       Z := Z+1
1536---     end
1537---   {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}

1539--- WORK IN CLASS
1540-

1542--- invariant, obtaining the following decorated program:
1543-

1545---   (2)  {{ 0*0 <= m /\ m<(0+1)*(0+1) }}
1546---           Z := 0
1547---   (3)            {{ Z*Z <= m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }};
1548---           while (Z+1)*(Z+1) <= X do
1549---   (4)            {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1)
1550---                            /\ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=X }} ->>          (c - WRONG!)
1551---   (5)            {{ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=m /\ m<((Z+1)+1)*((Z+1)+1) }}
1552---             Z := Z+1
1553---   (6)            {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}
1554---           end
1555---   (7)  {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) /\ ~((Z+1)*(Z+1)<=X) }} ->>    (b - OK)
1556---   (8)  {{ Z*Z<=m /\ m<(Z+1)*(Z+1) }}

1559--- condition (c), we see that the second conjunct of (4) is almost the same as
1560--- the first conjunct of (5), except that (4) mentions `X` while (5) mentions
1561--- `m`. But note that `X` is never assigned in this program, so we should
1562--- always have `X=m`. We didn't propagate this information from (1) into the
1563--- loop invariant, but we could!
1564-
1565--- Also, we don't need the second conjunct of (8), since we can obtain it from
1566--- the negation of the guard — the third conjunct in (7) — again under the

1568-

1572---   {{ X=m /\ 0*0 <= m }}
1573---     Z := 0
1574---                {{ X=m /\ Z*Z <= m }};
1575---     while (Z+1)*(Z+1) <= X do

1577---                {{ X=m /\ (Z+1)*(Z+1)<=m }}

1627-
1628--- Note to developers:
1629---     HIDE: CH: it might make sense to show all the variants for future

1633--- Here is a program that squares `X` by repeated addition:
1634-
1635---   {{ X = m }}
1636---     Y := 0;
1637---     Z := 0;
1638---     while Y <> X  do
1639---       Z := Z + X;
1640---       Y := Y + 1
1641---     end
1642---   {{ Z = m*m }}
1643-
1644--- WORK IN CLASS
1645-
1646--- The first thing to note is that the loop reads `X` but doesn't change its
1647--- value. As we saw in the previous example, it can be a good idea in such
1648--- cases to add `X = m` to the loop invariant. The other thing that we know is
1649--- often useful in the loop invariant is the postcondition, so let's add that
1650--- too, leading to the candidate loop invariant `Z = m * m /\ X = m`.
1651-
1652---   {{ X = m }} ->>                                       (a - WRONG)
1653---   {{ 0 = m*m /\ X = m }}
1654---     Y := 0
1655---                  {{ 0 = m*m /\ X = m }};
1656---     Z := 0
1657---                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }};
1658---     while Y <> X do
1659---                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m /\ Y <> X }} ->>   (c - WRONG)
1660---                  {{ Z+X = m*m /\ X = m }}
1661---       Z := Z + X
1662---                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }};
1663---       Y := Y + 1
1664---                  {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m }}
1665---     end
1666---   {{ Z = m*m /\ X = m /\ ~(Y <> X) }} ->>               (b - OK)
1667---   {{ Z = m*m }}
1668-
1669--- Conditions (a) and (c) fail because of the `Z = m*m` part. While `Z` starts
1670--- at `0` and works itself up to `m*m`, we can't expect `Z` to be `m*m` from
1671--- the start. If we look at how `Z` progresses in the loop, after the 1st
1672--- iteration `Z = m`, after the 2nd iteration `Z = 2*m`, and at the end
1673--- `Z = m*m`. Since the variable `Y` tracks how many times we go through the
1674--- loop, this leads us to derive a new loop invariant candidate:
1675--- `Z = Y*m /\ X = m`.
1676-
1677---   {{ X = m }} ->>                                        (a - OK)
1678---   {{ 0 = 0*m /\ X = m }}
1679---     Y := 0
1680---                   {{ 0 = Y*m /\ X = m }};
1681---     Z := 0
1682---                   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m }};
1683---     while Y <> X do
1684---                   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m /\ Y <> X }} ->>   (c - OK)
1685---                   {{ Z+X = (Y+1)*m /\ X = m }}
1686---       Z := Z + X
1687---                   {{ Z = (Y+1)*m /\ X = m }};
1688---       Y := Y + 1
1689---                   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m }}
1690---     end
1691---   {{ Z = Y*m /\ X = m /\ ~(Y <> X) }} ->>                (b - OK)
1692---   {{ Z = m*m }}
1693-
1694--- This new loop invariant makes the proof go through: all three conditions
1695--- are easy to check.
1696-
1697--- It is worth comparing the postcondition `Z = m*m` and the `Z = Y*m`
1698--- conjunct of the loop invariant. It is often the case that one has to
1699--- replace parameters with variables — or with expressions involving both
1700--- variables and parameters, like `m - Y` — when going from postconditions to
1701--- loop invariants.

1782--- ### Exercise (4 stars): factorial_correct (Advanced) ⭐⭐⭐⭐
1783-
1784--- Recall that `n!` denotes the factorial of `n` (i.e., `n! =
1785--- 1*2*...*n`). We
1786--- can define the factorial function recursively in Lean as follows:
1787-
1788-def fact : Nat → Nat
1789-  | 0 => 1
1790-  | Nat.succ n => Nat.succ n * fact n
1791-
1792-#eval fact 5
1793-
1794--- First, write the Imp program `factorial` that calculates the factorial of
1795--- the number initially stored in the variable `X` and puts it in the variable
1796--- `Y`.
1797-
1798--- Using your definition `factorial` and `slowAssignmentDec` as a guide, write
1799--- a formal decorated program `factorialDec` that implements the factorial
1800--- function. Ordinary Lean functions such as `fact` can be applied directly to
1801--- Imp variables inside assertions.
1802-
1803--- Fill in the blanks and finish the proof of correctness. Bear in mind that
1804--- we are working with natural numbers, for which both division and
1805--- subtraction can behave differently than with real numbers. Excluding both
1806--- operations from your loop invariant is advisable!
1807-
1808--- Then state a theorem named `factorial_correct` that says `factorialDec` is
1809--- correct, and prove the theorem. If all goes well, `verify` will leave you
1810--- with just two subgoals, each of which requires establishing some
1811--- mathematical property of `fact`, rather than proving anything about your
1812--- program.
1813-

1815--- how you could restate your assertions such that the mathematical operations
1816--- are more amenable to manipulation in Lean. For example, recall that
1817--- `1 + ...` is easier to work with than `... + 1`.

1829-    end
1830-      {{ Y * fact X = fact m ∧ X = 0 }}
1831-    ->> {{ Y = fact m }}
1832-  }
1833-})

1993--- Solution:
1994--- [[
1995---     {{ True }} ->>
1996---     {{ c = 0 + c /\ 0 = 0 }}
1997---   X := 0;
1998---     {{ c = X + c /\ 0 = 0 }}
1999---   Y := 0;
2000---     {{ c = X + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2001---   Z := c;
2002---     {{ Z = X + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2003---   while X <> a do
2004---       {{ Z = X + c /\ Y = 0 /\ X <> a }} ->>
2005---       {{ Z + 1 = X + 1 + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2006---     X := X + 1;
2007---       {{ Z + 1 = X + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2008---     Z := Z + 1
2009---       {{ Z = X + c /\ Y = 0 }}
2010---   end;
2011---     {{ Z = X + c /\ Y = 0 /\ ~(X <> a) }} ->>
2012---     {{ Z = a + Y + c }}
2013---   while Y <> b do
2014---       {{ Z = a + Y + c /\ Y <> b }} ->>
2015---       {{ Z + 1 = a + Y + 1 + c }}
2016---     Y := Y + 1;
2017---       {{ Z + 1 = a + Y + c }}
2018---     Z := Z + 1
2019---       {{ Z = a + Y + c }}
2020---   end
2021---     {{ Z = a + Y + c /\ ~(Y <> b) }} ->>
2022---     {{ Z = a + b + c }}
2023--- ]]

2031---         {{ c = 0 + 0 + c }}

2035---         {{ c = X + Y + c }}

2054---         {{ Z = a + Y + c }}
2055---     end
2056---       {{ Z = a + Y + c /\ ~(Y <> b) }} ->>

2160--- Note to developers:
2161---     `HIDE: Another (very) good exercise from 09-mid2 -- just needs typeset
2162---
2163---     The notion of weakest precondition has a natural dual : given a
2164---     precondition and a command, we can ask what is the strongest
2165---     postcondition of the command with respect to the
2166---     precondition. Formally, we can define it like this:
2167---
2168---     Q is the strongest postcondition of c for P if:
2169---
2170---     (a) {{P}} c {{Q}}, and
2171---
2172---     (b) if Q′ is an assertion such that {{P}}c{{Q′}},
2173---         then Q st implies Q′ st, for all states st.
2174---
2175---     Q is the strongest (most difficult to satisfy) assertion that is
2176---     guaranteed to hold after c if P holds before. For example, the
2177---     strongest postcondition of the command skip with respect to the
2178---     precondition Y = 1 is Y = 1. Similarly, the postcondition in...
2179---
2180---              {{ Y = y }}
2181---                if !Y === A0 then X := A0 else Y := !Y *** A2
2182---              {{ (Y = y = X = 0) ∨ (Y = 2*y ∧ y <> 0) }}
2183---
2184---     ...is the strongest one.
2185---
2186---     Complete each of the following Hoare triples with the strongest
2187---     postcondition for the given command and precondition.
2188---
2189---     (a) {{Y=1}} X:=!Y+++A1 {{?}}
2190---     (b) {{True}} X:=A5 {{?}}
2191---     (c) {{ True }} skip {{ ? }}
2192---     (d) {{ True }} while true do skip {{ ? }}
2193---     (e) {{ X = x ∧ Y = y }}
2194---         while BNot (!X === A0) do (
2195---                         Y := !Y +++ A2;
2196---                         X := !X --- A1
2197---                       )
2198---         {{ ? }}`

2405-/- It is easy to go from a `DCom` to a `Com` by erasing all
2406-annotations. -/

2408-def DCom.erase (d : DCom) : Com :=
2409-  match d with

2411-  | .seq d1 d2 => .seq d1.erase d2.erase
2412-  | .asgn x a => .asgn x a
2413-  | .cond b d1 d2 => .cond b d1.erase d2.erase

2427-def DCom.awp (post : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Assertion :=
2428-  match d with
2429-  | .skip => post
2430-  | .seq d1 d2 => d1.awp (d2.awp post)
2431-  | .asgn x a => {{ post [x ↦ ~a] }}
2432-  | .cond b d1 d2 =>
2433-      fun st =>
2434-        (b.eval st = true ∧ d1.awp post st) ∨
2435-        (b.eval st = false ∧ d2.awp post st)
2436-  | .whileDo _ invariant _ => invariant
2437-  | .assert assertion => fun st => assertion st ∧ post st
2438-
2439-def DCom.VerificationConditions
2440-    (post : Assertion) (d : DCom) : Prop :=
2441-  match d with
2442-  | .seq d1 d2 =>
2443-      d1.VerificationConditions (d2.awp post) ∧
2444-      d2.VerificationConditions post
2445-  | .cond _ d1 d2 =>
2446-      d1.VerificationConditions post ∧
2447-      d2.VerificationConditions post
2448-  | .whileDo b invariant body =>
2449-      (∀ st, invariant st ∧ b.eval st ≠ true → post st) ∧
2450-      (∀ st, invariant st ∧ b.eval st = true →
2451-        body.awp invariant st) ∧
2452-      body.VerificationConditions invariant
2453-  | _ => True
2454-
2455-theorem vc_correct (d : DCom) (post : Assertion)
2456-    (hvc : d.VerificationConditions post) :
2457-    ValidHoareTriple (d.awp post) d.erase post := by
2458-  sorry
2459-
2460-def Decorated.VerificationConditions
2461-    (dec : Decorated) : Prop :=
2462-  (dec.pre ->> dec.body.awp dec.post) ∧
2463-  dec.body.VerificationConditions dec.post
2464-
2465-theorem verification_correct (dec : Decorated)
2466-    (hvc : dec.VerificationConditions) :
2467-    dec.OuterTripleValid := by
2468-  sorry

2715--- ## Weakest Preconditions (Optional)
2716-
2717--- Note to developers:
2718---     HIDE: BCP 21: We talked about moving this stuff to the HoareAsLogic
2719---     chapter to lighten this chapter, but it fits awkwardly there, so I'm
2720---     leaving it here. It's optional anyway. We might consider assigning one
2721---     of the exercises as advanced-only though.
2722-
2723--- Some preconditions are more interesting than others. For example, the Hoare
2724--- triple
2725-
2726---   {{ False }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
2727-
2728--- is *not* very interesting: although it is perfectly valid, it tells us
2729--- nothing useful. Since the precondition isn't satisfied by any state, it
2730--- doesn't describe any situations where we can use the command `X := Y + 1`
2731--- to achieve the postcondition `X <= 5`.
2732-
2733--- By contrast,
2734-
2735---   {{ Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0 }}  X := Y + 1 {{ X <= 5 }}
2736-
2737--- has a useful precondition: it tells us that, if we can somehow create a
2738--- situation in which we know that `Y <= 4 /\ Z = 0`, then running this
2739--- command will produce a state satisfying the postcondition. However, this
2740--- precondition is not as useful as it could be, because the `Z = 0` clause in
2741--- the precondition actually has nothing to do with the postcondition
2742--- `X <= 5`.
2743-
2744--- The *most* useful precondition for this command is this one:
2745-
2746---   {{ Y <= 4 }}  X := Y + 1  {{ X <= 5 }}
2747-
2748--- The assertion `Y <= 4` is called the *weakest precondition* of `X := Y + 1`
2749--- with respect to the postcondition `X <= 5`.
2750-
2751--- Assertion `Y <= 4` is a *weakest precondition* of command `X := Y + 1` with
2752--- respect to postcondition `X <= 5`. Think of *weakest* here as meaning
2753--- "easiest to satisfy": a weakest precondition is one that as many states as
2754--- possible can satisfy.
2755-
2756--- `P` is a weakest precondition of command `c` for postcondition `Q` if
2757-
2758--- - `P` is a precondition, that is, `{{P}} c {{Q}}`; and
2759-
2760--- - `P` is at least as weak as all other preconditions, that is, if
2761---   `{{P'}} c {{Q}}` then `P' ->> P`.
2762-
2763--- Note that weakest preconditions need not be unique. For example, `Y <= 4`
2764--- was a weakest precondition above, but so are the logically equivalent
2765--- assertions `Y < 5`, `Y <= 2 * 2`, etc. It is easy to show that any two
2766--- weakest preconditions `P` and `P'` of a command `c` with respect to
2767--- postcondition `Q` are logically equivalent; that is, `P <<->> P'`.
2768-
2769-def IsWp (P : Assertion) (c : Com) (Q : Assertion) : Prop :=
2770-  ValidHoareTriple P c Q ∧
2771-  ∀ P' : Assertion, ValidHoareTriple P' c Q → P' ->> P
2772-
2773--- ### Exercise (1 star): wp ⭐
2774-
2775--- What are weakest preconditions of the following commands for the following
2776--- postconditions?
2777-
2778---   1) {{ ? }}  skip  {{ X = 5 }}
2779-
2780---   2) {{ ? }}  X := Y + Z {{ X = 5 }}
2781-
2782---   3) {{ ? }}  X := Y  {{ X = Y }}
2783-
2784---   4) {{ ? }}
2785---    if X = 0 then Y := Z + 1 else Y := W + 2 end
2786---    {{ Y = 5 }}
2787-
2788---   5) {{ ? }}
2789---    X := 5
2790---    {{ X = 0 }}
2791-
2792---   6) {{ ? }}
2793---    while true do X := 0 end
2794---    {{ X = 0 }}
2795-
2796---   1) X = 5
2797---   2) Y + Z = 5
2798---   3) True
2799---   4) (X = 0 /\ Z = 4) \/ (X <> 0 /\ W = 3)
2800---   5) False
2801---   6) True

2810-    IsWp ({{ Y ≤ 4 }}) (imp {X := Y + 1})

640622 -- At this point you may be wondering: which of these styles should I use by
641623 -- default?
642624 
643--- Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function,
644--- definitions are often simpler. When both styles are workable, relational
645--- definitions can be more elegant and easier to understand, and Lean
646--- generates useful inversion and induction principles from them. On the other
647--- hand, functional definitions are automatically deterministic and total --
648--- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove* these if we need them -- and we
649--- can use Lean's computation mechanism to simplify them during proofs.
625+-- Where the thing being defined is not easy to express as a function -- or is
626+-- genuinely *not* a function -- there is no real choice. When both styles are
627+-- workable, relational definitions can be more elegant and easier to
628+-- understand, and Lean generates useful inversion and induction principles
629+-- from them. On the other hand, functional definitions are automatically
630+-- deterministic and total -- whereas, for a relation, we must *prove* these
631+-- if we need them -- and we can use Lean's computation mechanism to simplify
632+-- them during proofs.
650633 
651634 -- In large developments it is common to give a definition in *both* styles
652635 -- plus a lemma that the two coincide, allowing later proofs to switch between
653--- points of view at will -- exactly what we did above in
654--- `Slang.Aexp.evalR_iff_eval` and `Slang.Bexp.evalR_iff_eval`.
